tip: Αγαπημένο μου (agapiméno mu) = my favorite; with an adjective in front, μου usually sits right after it, before the noun.
Κάνω κενό (káno kenó) is the phrase for having a free period: κάναμε κενό (káname kenó) = we had a free period.
Στο (sto) is σε and το fused together, since σε normally merges with the article after it: στο διάλειμμα (sto dhiálima) = at the break.
Σχολή (skholí) is a university school or department; σχολείο (skholío) is the kids' school. Same root, easy to mix up.
Greek has a verb for being late: άργησα να στείλω (áryisa na stílo) = I was late to send. No adjective needed, the verb carries the whole 'was late'.
Γράφω καλά (ghráfo kalá) = do well on a test, literally 'write well': έγραψα καλά (éghrapsa kalá) = I did well.
Οκτώ στα δέκα (októ sta dhéka) = eight out of ten; στα is how Greek says out of when you give a score.
Greek holds notes where English takes them: κρατάω σημειώσεις (kratáo simiósis) = literally 'I hold notes'.
Ιδιαίτερα (idhiétera) usually means especially, but κάνω ιδιαίτερα (káno idhiétera) = I give private lessons. Context decides which.
Masculine nouns ending in -ές usually take a -δες plural: ο καφές (o kafés) becomes καφέδες (kafédhes) = coffees, not the plain -ς swap you might expect.
Βάση (vási) means base, but in the exam system it is the admission cutoff: πέρασα τη βάση (pérasa ti vási) = I made the cutoff.
Αντιγράφω (andighráfo) means copy, and it is also the word for cheating on a test: αντιγραφή (andighrafí) = the cheating itself.
Doubling the negative is correct Greek: δεν κατάλαβα τίποτα (dhen katálava típota) = literally 'I didn't understand nothing', since τίποτα normally needs δεν with it.
Παρέα (paréa) means company or friend group; after a verb it means together: μελετάμε παρέα (meletáme paréa) = we study as a group.
Τα μαθήματά του (ta mathímatá tu) = his lessons, which for a school kid usually means his homework.
Απ' έξω (ap' ékso) = by heart, literally 'from outside'.
Όρεξη (óreksi) is literally appetite, and Greek stretches it to any desire: δεν έχω όρεξη (dhen ékho óreksi) = I don't feel like it.
Ορκωμοσία (orkomosía) = graduation ceremony, literally an oath-taking.
No word for of here: το βαριέμαι (to varyéme) takes a plain object, so Greek says 'I am bored it', not bored of it.
Πια (pia) at the end of a negative = not anymore: δεν βλέπω τηλεόραση πια (dhen vlépo tileórasi pia) = I don't watch TV anymore.
Όλα τα βλέπω (óla ta vlépo) names the object twice: όλα, then the little τα (ta). Fronting the object normally calls for that echo, it is not sloppy.
The internet fell: έπεσε το ίντερνετ (épese to ínternet) – a Greek service that goes down usually falls. Power too: έπεσε το ρεύμα (épese to révma).
Κολλάει (koláei) is literally 'it sticks', and a buffering video sticks in Greek. The same verb covers frozen apps and being stuck in traffic.
Downloads come down: κατέβασε (katévase) is literally 'bring it down'. Same verb for downloading apps, songs and files.
Ενημέρωση (enimérosi) = update, and in other contexts a briefing or the news.
Κινητό (kinitó) is literally 'the movable one', the everyday word for a mobile phone; τηλέφωνο (tiléfono) sounds more formal.
The battery finished, not you: μου τελείωσε η μπαταρία (mu telíose i bataría) = it ran out on me, with μου (mu) marking who it happened to.
You enter your account in Greek: μπήκα στον λογαριασμό (bíka ston logariasmó) – μπαίνω (béno) covers logging in and joining wi-fi.
The απο- (apo-) prefix usually undoes a verb: συνδέομαι (sindhéome) = log in, αποσυνδέομαι (aposindhéome) = log out, much like English un- or dis-.
Ανεβάζω/κατεβάζω (anevázo/katevázo) are literally take up and take down = upload/download: ανέβασα μια φωτογραφία (anévasa mia fotoghrafía) = I posted a photo.
